## Message to the owner

**Subject: The 30% line — can't write it as is, but here's what we can say**

I'm not going to give you "our new website drove 30% sales growth" — not because the math is wrong, but because that comparison is measuring autumn, not the website. Here's the problem, and then three lines that work.

**The 30% is the normal September-to-October ramp**

| | September | October | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2025** (no website change) | $90,000 | $115,200 | **+28.0%** |
| **2026** (website launched Oct 1) | $100,000 | $130,000 | **+30.0%** |

Last year the business did a 28% September-to-October jump with no new website at all. So roughly 28 of those 30 points are just the season — this is the month the business always ramps. The website year is only about 2 points ahead of the pattern that was already there.

**The like-for-like comparison is year over year, and it's 12.8%**

October 2026 vs October 2025: $130,000 vs $115,200 = **+12.8%**. That's a good number — it's real growth. But September was already running +11.1% year over year ($100,000 vs $90,000), so October is only ~1.7 points ahead of the trend the business was on before the site went live.

If I do a rough seasonal adjustment — apply last year's 28% ramp to this September — I'd expect about $128,000 in October. We got $130,000. That's roughly $2,000, or about 1.5% of October sales, above what seasonality alone predicts. That is a promising signal, but it is a back-of-envelope figure, not a measurement of the website, and I wouldn't put it on a board slide as proof. October is also one month, and one month is noise: a couple of large orders or a weather week moves it.

**Why this matters beyond being fussy:** board members saw last October's numbers. If we claim 30% attributable to the website and someone asks what October 2025 did, the answer is "+28%, before the website," and the credibility hit lands on you, not on the slide. If we have outside investors or lenders, an unsupportable causal claim in the minutes is also the kind of thing that gets read back to us later.

**Three lines that hold up**

1. *Factual, leads with the real number:*
"New website launched October 1. October sales of $130,000, up 12.8% year over year and 30% over September, in line with our normal autumn ramp. Full read after Q4."

2. *If you want the launch framed as momentum, not proof:*
"Website launched October 1 into a strong quarter: October sales $130,000, +12.8% YoY, our best October yet. Contribution will be assessed against a full seasonal cycle in January."

3. *Shortest, all defensible:*
"October sales $130,000, +12.8% vs. last October. New site live since October 1; Q4 will tell us what it's adding."

My pick is #1 or #3 — they give you the growth story without asking the board to believe something we can't show.

**If you want a claim about the website itself,** I can set up the measurement properly: compare Oct–Dec 2026 YoY against the Jan–Sep 2026 YoY trend, and check whether sessions, conversion rate, and average order value moved in a way that matches a site change rather than a demand change. A holdout — keep the old site on a slice of traffic or in one region for a few weeks — would give us something close to causal. Say the word and I'll scope it; we'd have a defensible number by the January board rather than a soft one now.

Tell me which line you want and I'll format it into the deck.
